headline: LayerZero V2 Endpoint defaults are controlled by 3-of-5 OneSig owner contracts with no on-chain timelock observed.

findings.text: The assessed Ethereum EndpointV2 owner is 0xBe010A7e3686FdF65E93344ab664D065A0B02478. Arbitrum and Unichain EndpointV2 surfacers show separate OneSig owners at 0x9A3cE220D17a92dd4DF9766ceE48fDd0c448bA4f and 0x32b323EFC09D5812510B6510b242647C603947Ab.

The assessed EndpointV2 is not evidenced as a proxy in the fetched reads, but it has owner-controlled mutable configuration: MessageLibManager exposes onlyOwner functions to register libraries and set default send and receive libraries.

The observed fast path is OneSig threshold signatures plus executor execution. The Ethereum OneSig threshold is 3 and totalSigners is 5; no on-chain timelock constant was observed in the fetched OneSig surface.

The Ethereum, Arbitrum, and Unichain OneSig contracts expose the same threshold shape, 3-of-5 signers, and executorRequired=true. The signer real-world identities were not verified, so these multisigs do not meet the Security Council standard.
No on-chain Governor or token-voting path was found in fetched evidence for the assessed EndpointV2 control path. The operative owner path is OneSig.

No separate emergency guardian was verified. The relevant emergency-like surface is the owner-configurable message library path, including default library controls and the presence of BlockedMessageLib in registered libraries.

The highest reachable tier is treated as T1/T2 for the assessed messaging core because the owner can register and set default message libraries, which can affect default cross-chain message verification and delivery for OApps using defaults. The path is controlled by a 3-of-5 OneSig with no observed on-chain delay.

steelman.red: The red case is that a small multisig can change default message libraries without an observed timelock, which is a high-blast-radius control path for a bridge/messaging protocol.
steelman.orange: The orange case is strongest: the path is not a single EOA or 2-of-3, but it is still a 3-of-5 multisig that fails the Security Council standard and controls economically or fund-critical messaging configuration without a verified exit window.
steelman.green: The green case is that EndpointV2 code appears immutable rather than proxy-upgradeable, and OApps can configure their own libraries instead of relying on protocol defaults.

rationale.verdict: Choosing orange because T1/T2 messaging configuration control is reachable through a 3-of-5 OneSig path with no on-chain delay observed; it is not red because the controlling actor is not a single EOA, not a 2-of-3 multisig, and the core code itself was not shown to be proxy-upgradeable.

evidence.shows: Ethereum EndpointV2 surfacer, owner() returning 0xBe010A7e3686FdF65E93344ab664D065A0B02478, registered libraries including BlockedMessageLib, SendUln302, ReceiveUln302, and ReadLib1002, and write methods including registerLibrary, setDefaultSendLibrary, setDefaultReceiveLibrary, setLzToken, recoverToken, and transferOwnership.

Ethereum OneSig surfacer showing executorRequired=true, executor 0x39f86ECef62c5bcE23428d6b7c7050D9Ecb0e346, five signers, threshold 3, totalSigners 5, and write method executeTransaction.
Content-pinned Ethereum OneSig threshold() read returning 3.
Content-pinned Ethereum OneSig totalSigners() read returning 5.
Content-pinned Ethereum OneSig getSigners() read returning five signer addresses.

Source shows onlyOwner functions registerLibrary, setDefaultSendLibrary, setDefaultReceiveLibrary, and setDefaultReceiveLibraryTimeout, while OApp-specific library selection uses _assertAuthorized(_oapp).

Official deployed-contracts documentation describes EndpointV2 as the primary entrypoint for cross-chain communications and configuration management, with SendUln302, ReceiveUln302, LZ Executor, Dead DVN, and BlockedMessageLib roles.
Etherscan code page shows EndpointV2 source code verified as an exact match.

unknowns: C1: Base EndpointV2 owner() read failed in the fetched surfacer due RPC rate limiting, and most chains in the address book were not individually re-read.
C3: No MIN_DELAY or timelock-style constant was found on the assessed OneSig owner contracts, but any off-chain signing policy delay was not verified.
C4: OneSig signer identities and insider versus non-insider classification were not verified.

C5: No Governor path was found in fetched evidence; proposal threshold, voting period, quorum, and queue-to-execute delay are therefore not determined for any off-chain or token governance process that may exist.
C6: Emergency-only roles beyond the EndpointV2 owner-configured library path were not exhaustively checked across all message libraries and chains.

headline: No canonical user withdrawal surface was identified on EndpointV2; OApp-level exits were not assessed.

findings.text: The assessed EndpointV2 write surface includes send, clear, burn, nilify, recoverToken, and message-library configuration functions, but no withdraw, redeem, claim, requestWithdrawal, or exit function was identified on the EndpointV2 surfacer.
EndpointV2 source shows send is external payable, clear requires OApp authorization through _assertAuthorized(_oapp), and recoverToken plus setLzToken are onlyOwner.

Direct contract interaction is visible through surfacer and Etherscan write-method listings, but that does not establish a user-facing exit path because the LayerZero core is a messaging endpoint rather than a custody vault.

rationale.verdict: Choosing unknown because the assessed EndpointV2 does not expose a canonical custody exit function, while LayerZero-connected asset bridges and OApps can have separate withdrawal, claim, mint, burn, or unlock semantics that were not assessed in this run.

evidence.shows: Ethereum EndpointV2 write-method surface lists burn, clear, lzCompose, lzReceive, nilify, recoverToken, registerLibrary, send, setConfig, setDefaultReceiveLibrary, setDefaultReceiveLibraryTimeout, setDefaultSendLibrary, setDelegate, setLzToken, setReceiveLibrary, setReceiveLibraryTimeout, setSendLibrary, skip, transferOwnership, and verify.
EndpointV2 source shows send(...) external payable, clear(...) authenticating the OApp, and onlyOwner controls for setLzToken and recoverToken.
Official documentation describes EndpointV2 as the primary entrypoint for cross-chain communications and configuration management, not as a canonical asset vault.

unknowns: E1: No user-facing withdraw, redeem, claim, requestWithdrawal, or exit function was located on assessed EndpointV2, but exits for OApps, OFTs, Stargate-style assets, or app-specific bridges were not enumerated.
E2: Access modifiers and pause guards for OApp-level exit functions were not assessed.
E3: Pause role holders for any app-level request-placement or claim-finalized funds flow were not identified.
E4: Governance versus emergency pause semantics for OApp-level exits were not assessed.
E5: Finalized funds claimability under pause could not be determined because no canonical finalized-funds claim function was identified on EndpointV2.
E6: Insolvency, buffer, queue, or rate-limit constraints are not applicable to the assessed EndpointV2 itself but may exist in asset bridge applications using LayerZero.
E7: Direct contract access was observed for EndpointV2, but direct exit access could not be classified without selecting a concrete OApp or token bridge.

headline: LayerZero V2 depends on DVNs, executors, and configurable message libraries, but the live dependency quorum and fallback model were not fully verified.

findings.text: Official docs and repository text describe LayerZero V2 as a cross-chain messaging protocol using configurable DVNs and executors, with SendUln302 and ReceiveUln302 message libraries and an LZ Executor contract.
The repository states that executors deliver messages for a fee, which implies a relayer/executor dependency for automatic delivery.
EndpointV2 owner-controlled defaults can change message libraries, so part of the dependency surface is governance or admin mutable.

rationale.verdict: Choosing unknown because the fetched evidence establishes real external dependencies, DVNs, executors, message libraries, and owner-configurable defaults, but not enough on-chain evidence was collected to classify the live quorum, fallback, censorship, degradation, and mutability properties across the deployed network.

evidence.shows: Repository README describes LayerZero V2 as an omnichain interoperability protocol where applications can configure any number of Decentralized Verifier Networks and where executors deliver messages for a fee.
Official deployed-contracts documentation describes EndpointV2, SendUln302, ReceiveUln302, LZ Executor, Dead DVN, and Blocked Message Library roles.
MessageLibManager source shows owner-controlled default send and receive library settings and OApp-authorized per-app library selection.
Ethereum EndpointV2 surfacer shows registered libraries and the owner-controlled write-method surface for configuring message libraries.

unknowns: A1: External contract calls and live dependencies were not exhaustively enumerated across EndpointV2, message libraries, DVNs, executors, and all chains.
A2: DVN committee size, quorum, signer membership, fault threshold, and selection process were not read from live contracts in this run.
A3: The bridge or messaging trust model was identified at a high level, but the exact default verifier set and quorum for each route were not verified on-chain.
A4: Nested collateral or asset custody dependencies are not applicable to EndpointV2 itself, but OApp and token bridge dependencies were not assessed.
A5: DeFiLlama forkedFrom or clone metadata was not fetched or verified.
A6: Fallback, circuit-breaker, timeout, and blocked-library behavior were only partially identified; their exact operational limits were not fully verified.
A7: Sequencer, appchain, and chain-specific liveness dependencies were not assessed for all supported chains.
A8: Executor permissionlessness, censorship resistance, and user fallback to manual execution were not fully verified.
A9: The mutability and governance of dependency configuration across every deployed endpoint and route were not fully assessed.

headline: EndpointV2 send is externally callable, and the official materials describe the protocol as permissionless public-blockchain infrastructure.

findings.text: EndpointV2 source shows send(...) is external payable. The fetched code did not show an owner whitelist on this send entry point.
Executors and DVNs are dependencies for delivery and verification, but the fetched send entry point itself is not evidenced as operator-gated.
The official website describes LayerZero as permissionless infrastructure, and the repository describes the protocol as immutable, censorship-resistant, and permissionless messaging infrastructure.
An independent contract path is available through public contracts: Etherscan and DeFiPunkd expose EndpointV2 read/write surfaces, and source shows direct send(...) access.

No contract-level sanctions or address blocklist was identified in the fetched EndpointV2 send path. The official terms impose site/legal eligibility restrictions, including sanctions restrictions, but those are not evidenced as a smart-contract gate.
The assessed EndpointV2 public write-method surface includes send, and the source marks send as external payable.
LayerZero terms restrict use of the Site by sanctioned persons or jurisdictions, while separately describing the Protocol as source-available software running on public distributed blockchains.

steelman.red: The red case would require evidence of contract-level allowlists, KYC, sanctions blocks, or operator-only user entry points; that was not found for EndpointV2 send.
steelman.orange: The orange case is that website terms restrict certain users and message execution depends on infrastructure such as executors and DVNs, which can affect practical access.
steelman.green: The green case is strongest: the core send function is external payable, official materials describe the protocol as permissionless public-blockchain infrastructure, and no protocol-level whitelist was found in the assessed send path.

rationale.verdict: Choosing green because the assessed contract-level user entry point send(...) is externally callable without a fetched whitelist gate, while the observed restrictions are site/legal terms rather than a protocol-enforced access control.

evidence.shows: EndpointV2 source shows send(...) external payable and owner-only controls only for functions such as setLzToken and recoverToken.
Ethereum EndpointV2 surfacer lists public write methods including send and administrative methods separately.
Official website describes LayerZero as permissionless infrastructure for issuing, connecting, and expanding assets, products, or ideas across blockchains.
Repository README describes LayerZero V2 as an immutable, censorship-resistant, and permissionless messaging protocol for blockchains.
Terms include eligibility and sanctions restrictions for use of the Site, and separately describe the Protocol as source-available software running on public distributed blockchains.
Etherscan exposes the verified EndpointV2 contract page and public contract interaction surface.

unknowns: A1: Only the assessed EndpointV2 send path was reviewed; all possible user-facing functions across all chains and OApps were not exhaustively checked.
A4: A full repository-wide and all-contract sanctions or blocklist grep was not performed; the statement is limited to the fetched EndpointV2 send path.

headline: Core contracts are verified and public source exists, but audit-to-deployment coverage and post-audit drift were not pinned.

findings.text: Ethereum EndpointV2 and the Ethereum OneSig owner contract both show Etherscan source-code verification as exact matches.

LayerZero-Labs/LayerZero-v2 is a public GitHub repository, and fetched source files include EndpointV2.sol and MessageLibManager.sol, but no specific commit SHA was pinned or locally compile-matched in this run.

The official LayerZero-Labs/Audits repository includes an Endpoint V2 - EVM / EndpointV2 folder listing multiple Dec 2023 audit PDFs, including reports named for Zellic, Certora, OtterSec, Paladin, Blockian, CMichel, and Windhustler.

At least some audit firms listed in the official audits repository, including Zellic and Certora, are recognized security review firms; individual PDF contents and scopes were not opened and verified in this run.
Audit reports listed are dated Dec 2023, while the assessment date is 2026-06-22. Post-audit drift between reviewed source and the deployed verified contracts was not established.

The assessed Ethereum EndpointV2 is a verified direct contract in fetched evidence, and the owner read provenance did not identify a proxy implementation; however, proxy and implementation status for all chain deployments and auxiliary contracts was not exhaustively checked.

steelman.red: The red case is that the pinned protocol context recorded no audit links and this run did not pin an exact commit or compile reproduction for the deployed bytecode.
steelman.orange: The orange case is strongest: verified deployed source and public repos exist, and official audit folders were discovered, but exact audit scope, commit coverage, and drift to current deployed contracts remain unresolved.
steelman.green: The green case is that EndpointV2 and OneSig are verified exact-match contracts, the source repository is public, and multiple EndpointV2 audit reports are publicly listed in an official LayerZero-Labs audit repository.

rationale.verdict: Choosing orange because the core verified-source and official audit repository evidence is meaningful, but the run did not verify audit PDF contents, exact reviewed commits, deployment coverage across chains, or post-audit drift.

evidence.shows: Etherscan shows EndpointV2 source code verified as an exact match.
Etherscan shows OneSig source code verified as an exact match.

unknowns: V2: No exact Git commit SHA was pinned for the deployed verified EndpointV2 source in this run.
V2: Local compilation and bytecode reproduction were not performed.
V3: Audit PDFs were discovered in an official repository, but the PDFs were not opened, screenshotted, or parsed, so exact scope, commit, findings, and remediation status remain unverified.
V5: Post-audit drift between Dec 2023 audit material and contracts live at the 2026-06-22 assessment date was not determined.
V6: Proxy and implementation status was not exhaustively checked for all LayerZero V2 deployments, message libraries, executors, DVNs, and owner contracts across every chain in the address book.
